en: The Therāpadāna,
Buddhavagga 2.
The Apadāna of the Paccekabuddhas
Now, listen to the legend of the Paccekabuddhas:
“The sage of Videha, with his body bent, questioned the Tathāgata as he dwelt in Jeta’s Grove.”
"O Hero, by what causes do those known as Paccekabuddhas come to be?
Then the Great Seer, the Supreme Omniscient One, said:
With a sweet voice, he spoke these auspicious words to Ānanda:
“Those who have performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas,
yet have not attained liberation within the teachings of the Conquerors.”
By that very means of spiritual urgency, the wise—
possessing exceedingly sharp wisdom even without Buddhas—
[attain] through even a limited object [of meditation].
They attain the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha.
In the entire world, excluding myself,
there is no one equal to the paccekabuddhas.
I shall properly declare this mere portion of the praise of those great sages,
the Buddhas themselves.
Excellent words are like honey to the small-minded;
desiring the unsurpassed medicine,
listen with hearts full of faith toward all.
The successive proclamations made by the Paccekabuddhas when they had gathered together,
as well as the danger [of defilements] and the basis for dispassion—
And how they attained enlightenment:
Perceiving dispassion in things that provoke passion,
their minds were detached from a world full of lust.
Having abandoned conceptual proliferations and the flickerings of the mind,
they likewise attained enlightenment.
Having laid aside the rod toward all living beings, they reached that state.
Without harming even one among them,
compassionate and seeking their welfare with a mind of loving-kindness,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having laid aside the rod toward all beings,
and not harming even one among them,
he would desire neither a son, much less a friend.
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who has become intimate with others, affections arise;
from these affections, this suffering comes into being.
Seeing the peril born of affection,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Feeling compassion for friends and dear ones...
One whose mind is bound fails to achieve his goal;
seeing this danger in intimacy,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Just as one who is entangled like a wide-spreading bamboo creeper,
so too is the attachment toward children and wives;
but like a bamboo shoot that does not cling to the stalk, [one should remain unattached].
One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Just as an unbound deer in the forest goes wherever it desires for its pasture, so should one go.
“A wise man, looking for peace,
should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“There is conversation in the midst of companions;”
In dwelling, standing, walking, or on a journey—
observing with equanimity that which is not craved—
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“There is delight in play among companions,
and there is great affection for one’s children;
being loathsome toward separation from what is dear, [one seeks to escape it].”
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Being equanimous toward the four quarters, one should be free from resentment,
content with whatever comes.
Enduring hardships, undaunted,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Some who have gone forth are difficult to restrain;”
Moreover, even while living as a householder in a home,
being unconcerned with the children of others,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Having cast off the marks of a householder,
like a *koviḷāra* tree with its leaves completely stripped away,
the Hero, having severed the bonds of household life, [has gone forth].”
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
If one should find a prudent companion who walks together with one, a steadfast person of noble conduct, then one may walk with them.
“Having overcome all dangers,
one should wander, contented and mindful.
But if one does not find a wise companion...”
Walking together with one who lives virtuously and is steadfast,
like a king abandoning a conquered kingdom,
one should wander alone like an elephant in the Matanga forest.
"Truly, we praise the excellence of companions;
one should associate with those who are superior and equal.
Not finding such, one should live on blameless food."
One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Having seen those golden, radiant [bracelets],
well-finished by a smith’s son;
"Though two [arms] may be joined together on one arm,
let one wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
'In this way, may I have no companion.'"
Or verbal expression, or even provocation;
seeing this danger in the future,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Sensual pleasures are indeed variegated, sweet, and delightful;
they agitate the mind with their diverse forms.
Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, [one should turn away from them].”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Calamity, swelling, affliction,
disease, the arrow, and fear— these are [the evils].”
Seeing this danger in the strands of sensual pleasure,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Cold and heat, hunger and thirst—
Wind and heat, gadflies and serpents—
having overcome all these,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Like a bull elephant who has left the herds behind,
with his shoulders well-developed and majestic as a lotus,
he dwells in the forest just as he pleases.
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“That is impossible for one who delights in company,
that he should experience temporary liberation;”
Having heeded the words of the Kinsman of the Sun,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros,
having transcended the thorns of speculative views.
I have attained the certainty of rightness and realized the path;
having arisen in knowledge, I am no longer led by others.
I shall wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having become free from greed, free from deceit, free from thirst,
free from hypocrisy, with taints and delusion wiped away,
and without expectations in the whole world—
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
One should avoid a wicked companion who sees no harm and is intent on what is wrong.
One should not associate with one who is addicted to sensual pleasures or heedless;
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
One should cultivate friendship with one who is learned and a bearer of the Dhamma.
A friend who is noble and eloquent,
having understood the meanings and dispelled doubt—
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Without adorning himself with play, delight, or sensual pleasure in the world,
and being free from longing; abstaining from the grounds for ornamentation, he is a speaker of truth.”
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
[Leaving behind] son and wife, father and mother,
wealth and grain, and kinsmen—
"Having abandoned all sensual pleasures as they arise, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
This is a fetter; here there is but little happiness."
The gratification is slight, while suffering here is much greater;
knowing this to be a mere snare,
the wise man should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having torn asunder the fetters,
like a water-dwelling fish breaking through a net,
he does not turn back, like a fire that has consumed its fuel.
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros—
eyes cast down, not fickle with the feet,
with the sense-faculties guarded and the mind protected.
“Unflooded and unburning,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having cast off the marks of a householder,
Like the Pārichatta tree with its dense foliage,
clad in saffron robes, having gone forth,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Not greedy for flavors, not lustful,
not supporting others, wandering from house to house with a mind unattached to family after family.
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having abandoned the five hindrances that defile the mind,
having dispelled all mental impurities;
“Unattached, one should cut off the fault of affection;
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Having cast behind one both pleasure and pain...”
Having long since abandoned both joy and grief,
having attained equanimity and purified tranquility,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Aroused in energy for the attainment of the supreme goal,
with an undaunted mind and untiring conduct,
firm in exertion and endowed with fortitude and strength— ”
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Constantly delighting in seclusion and meditation,
one should always practice in accordance with the Dhamma among all phenomena.
Having comprehended the peril in states of existence,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Striving with diligence, longing for the destruction of craving...
Not stammering, learned, and mindful;
having fully understood the Dhamma, resolute and striving,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Like a lion untroubled by sounds,
like the wind unentangled in a net,
like a lotus unsullied by water—
“One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Like a powerful fanged lion, having overpowered [all],
the king of beasts wanders triumphant.”
"Frequent secluded lodgings;
wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Cultivate loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and liberation."
Cultivating joy at the proper time,
and not coming into conflict with the whole world,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion,
and having torn asunder the fetters,
one who does not tremble at the dissolution of life—
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
People associate and serve others for a purpose;
friends without a motive are rare these days.
People who possess wisdom regarding their own welfare are impure;
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros—
those whose virtue is purified and whose wisdom is thoroughly cleansed.
Concentrated and devoted to wakefulness,
possessing insight and seeing the distinction between phenomena,
one should be known as one who has entered upon the factors of the path and the factors of enlightenment.
Having cultivated emptiness, the wishless,
and likewise the signless within the teaching of the Victor,
those wise ones do not fall back into the state of mere disciples.
They become Paccekabuddhas, self-become ones.
Possessing the Great Dhamma and a manifold body of Dhamma,
they are masters of their own minds and have crossed over the flood of all suffering.
With uplifted minds, seeing the supreme goal,
like lions, like the tips of rhinoceros horns,
with peaceful faculties, peaceful minds, and concentrated.
Among the beings of the borderlands, practicing their respective ways,
the Paccekabuddhas— shining here on this island and elsewhere—
are constantly intent on the welfare of others.
Having abandoned all obscurations, O lords of men,
you are lamps for the world with the radiance of dense gold;
without doubt, you are the most worthy of offerings in the world.
The Paccekabuddhas, ever well-satisfied,
cause the well-spoken words of the Paccekabuddhas to circulate throughout the world together with its devas.
Those fools who, having heard such words, do not act accordingly,
wander again and again through sufferings.
[This is] the well-spoken teaching of the Paccekabuddhas.
Just as one hears of honey trickling down from a small crevice,
so too those who apply themselves to practice become possessors of wisdom and seers of truth.
The sublime discourses spoken by the Paccekabuddhas and the Conquerors after their renunciation—
those were proclaimed by the Lion of the Sakyans, the Supreme among Men.
These transformations of the Paccekabuddhas were manifested out of compassion for the world,
for the purpose of making known the Dhamma.
“These were proclaimed by the Lion of the Self-Existent Ones for the purpose of increasing the accumulation of thoughts of spiritual urgency.
Thus ends the *Paccekabuddhāpadāna*.
